title: Why Ice Cream Gives You a 30-Second Headache 🍦
description:
Why does ice cream give you brain freeze? Cold on the roof of your mouth makes a big artery behind your eyes open wide, the rush of blood raises pressure, and your trigeminal nerve sends the pain to your forehead, which is why brain freeze fades in under 30 seconds.

Sources:
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/04/120422231742.htm
https://www.healthline.com/health/sphenopalatine-ganglioneuralgia-brain-freeze
https://sciencenotes.org/brain-freeze-ice-cream-headache-causes-symptoms-and-prevention/

Animated in the Kawaii Anime style.

topic: Why does ice cream give you brain freeze?
script:
Ice cream gives you a 30-second headache,
but your brain never freezes.
So what's going on?
It starts on the roof of your mouth.
It's packed with nerves and blood vessels,
and ice cream chills it super fast.
Scientists think a big artery behind your eyes
suddenly opens wide,
to rush in warm blood.
That flood of blood
pushes up the pressure inside your head.
Your trigeminal nerve feels it,
but it gets mixed up,
and sends the pain to your forehead instead.
That's called referred pain.
Once things warm up,
the artery narrows again,
and the ache fades, usually in under 30 seconds.
Want it gone faster?
Press your warm tongue
to the roof of your mouth.
Honestly, your head's just overreacting to dessert.
So which hits you harder:
ice cream or a slushie?
key_facts: Cold on the palate triggers a sudden dilation of the anterior cerebral artery and a rush of blood flow; pain eases as it constricts (Serrador et al. 2012, via ScienceDaily)
Increased blood flow is thought to raise pressure inside the skull (ScienceDaily 2012)
The trigeminal nerve relays the signal and the pain is felt in the forehead: referred pain (Healthline)
Brain freeze usually lasts under about 30 seconds (Science Notes, Healthline)
Pressing the tongue or thumb to the roof of the mouth warms it and helps it pass (Healthline)
